title: Rebuke with love (Leviticus 19:17)
hookLine: "thou shalt surely rebuke thy neighbor", gently and privately
tomorrow: Aaron ended fights by visiting each side alone. what did he say?

lines: THE GROUP CHAT IS DRAFTING SOMETHING.
cards: A friend has been late to every practice for two weeks, and everyone has noticed. The group chat is drafting something; you can feel it coming.
Leviticus has a verse for this exact moment: "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart; thou shalt surely rebuke thy neighbour, and not bear sin because of him." Surely rebuke. Not maybe.
And yet some sages say: sometimes, hush. Two real views, and both come from people who love the verse.

teach.b: The word is tochachah: rebuke. The first view says: speak. Look at the verse's order.
Don't hate in your heart, then rebuke. Swallowing it is how the grudge starts. How many times?
The Talmud says: even a hundred. And the verse's last words, not bear sin because of him, the rabbis read as a warning: don't shame him while you do it.
Maimonides spells it out: in private, softly, for the other person's good. The second view says: sometimes, hush.

teach.h: HUSH: IF IT WON'T BE HEARD.
teach.b: The Talmud keeps a teaching that just as it's a mitzvah to say what will be heard, it's a mitzvah not to say what won't be. And it remembers two sages being honest about their own day.
Rabbi Tarfon: I wonder if anyone now can take rebuke. Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah: I wonder if anyone now knows how to give it. Notice what the two views share.
Neither says post it for everyone.
Neither says keep the grudge. They differ on timing and on the listener: speak gently, again and again, or wait until it can be heard.
Something to tell a friend tonight: an ancient sage worried that nobody in his generation knew how to criticize well.

how: Jewish teaching on tochachah, from Leviticus 19:17 through the Talmud and Maimonides, asks for concerns to be raised privately and gently, without shaming; some teachers add that it's better to wait when the words won't be heard.

o: a punishment a teacher hands to a student
a public warning so others won't do the same
a gentle, private word to set something right

games.q: speak, or hush — tap the pairs.
p: don't hate in your heart; rebuke
who knows how to give rebuke?

s: the verse puts 'don't hate in your heart' right before 'rebuke'
Leviticus 19:17: speaking up is how a grudge doesn't start.
tochachah means calling someone out in front of everyone
the rabbis read the verse as a warning against shaming; Maimonides says in private, softly.
one Talmud teaching says it's a mitzvah not to say what won't be heard
and another says rebuke even a hundred times. both views live in the tradition.

games.q: a friend tells you: don't say anything to her about it, she won't listen anyway. you disagree. what's the strongest case for your friend's side?
o: a teaching that it's a mitzvah not to say what won't be heard.
the verse only asks you to rebuke strangers, never your friends.
the verse says to rebuke once; after one try, you're done.
games.why: the hush view rests on the Talmud's teaching about words that won't be heard. the speak view answers: even a hundred times, gently and in private.

practice: Bring to mind one concern you've been holding about someone, the kind that's turning into a grudge. Write it by hand in one sentence: start with something you value about them, then the concern, plainly, with no always or never.
Fold it; it's for a quiet conversation, not a group chat.

wordCard.voice: Tochachah: rebuke, given privately and gently, so the other person can hear it and nobody is shamed.

orig.note: Hebrew: rebuke, reproof; Leviticus 19:17 says hokheach tokhiach, surely rebuke.

carryVoice: Your line: rebuke with love. Quietly, privately, and only as loud as it can be heard. That's today.

sources.q: Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart; thou shalt surely rebuke thy neighbour, and not bear sin because of him.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Arakhin 16b (rebuke even if not accepted; 'not bear sin because of him' as not shaming; Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah on who can take and give rebuke)
Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 31a (hokheach tokhiach: even a hundred times)
Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 65b (as it is a mitzvah to say what will be heard, so it is a mitzvah not to say what will not be heard)
Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot De'ot 6:7 (rebuke privately, gently, for the other's good)
